description: Gold standard claim examples built from explicit user feedback. Used to validate the judge — run coverletter extract --validate-judge to check judge accuracy against these.

examples.label: approved
examples.claim_text: At BritBox, I owned the VideoViewEvents pipeline end-to-end
examples.source_note: Ownership claim at the right level — specific employer, specific system, ownership verb

examples.label: approved
examples.claim_text: At BritBox, I determined what 'watch duration' meant at the subscriber grain before any engineering began
examples.source_note: Decision-level claim — this is requirements definition work, matchable to 'data modeling' and 'requirements translation' JD requirements

examples.label: approved
examples.claim_text: At Universe, I built the dbt environment from scratch
examples.source_note: Ownership + build claim, employer-specific, right abstraction level

examples.label: approved
examples.claim_text: At BritBox, I had full admin access in AWS and owned the full infrastructure setup — EC2, IAM roles, Glue jobs, and DynamoDB metadata tracking
examples.source_note: Scope/ownership claim across cloud services — right level, specific employer

examples.label: approved
examples.claim_text: At UNITE HERE, I built data catalogs to track distinct definitions across locals on national campaigns
examples.source_note: Ownership claim, employer-specific, specific deliverable

examples.label: approved
examples.claim_text: For my personal project CBA Clock, I built an 8-task Airflow DAG that takes a collective bargaining agreement from raw PDF to structured, queryable data
examples.source_note: Personal project claim — context type is 'project' not 'employer'. CBA Clock is NOT an employer. The phrase 'For my personal project' must appear or the context must be 'project'.

examples.label: approved
examples.claim_text: At BritBox, I was the primary engineer on the Amazon platform viewership pipeline covering millions of users
examples.source_note: Ownership claim — Amazon here is a data source/partner, not the employer. BritBox is the employer. Claim correctly grounded.

examples.label: approved
examples.claim_text: At Universe, I introduced Great Expectations alongside dbt so documentation, definitions, and lineage were connected in one place
examples.source_note: Decision + build claim — specific tooling decision with a stated purpose

examples.label: rejected
examples.claim_text: I have experience with event-based data
examples.source_note: Too generic — this is a capability statement, not a claim. Cannot be matched to a specific JD requirement. Not grounded in any employer.

examples.label: rejected
examples.claim_text: I work comfortably in both Airflow and dbt
examples.source_note: Capability statement — says nothing about what was built or owned. 'Work comfortably in X' is not a claim.

examples.label: rejected
examples.claim_text: At CBA Clock, I built an 8-task Airflow DAG
examples.source_note: Wrong context type — CBA Clock is a personal project, not an employer. The context must be 'project', not 'employer'. This is a hallucinated employer attribution.

examples.label: rejected
examples.claim_text: I have been able to figure myself out and get up to speed in all four cloud environments
examples.source_note: Not a claim about what was built or owned — it's a self-assessment about adaptability. Cannot be matched to a JD requirement. The real claims are the specific employer-grounded ownership statements ('At X, I owned Y in cloud Z') — this sentence is a summary of those claims, not a claim itself.

examples.label: rejected
examples.claim_text: I have never needed a ramp period when a new cloud environment was the requirement
examples.source_note: Too generic and framed as a negative ('never needed'). Not a claim about what was built. The user explicitly corrected this framing during a session.

examples.label: rejected
examples.claim_text: The VideoViewEvents pipeline processed play, pause, seek, heartbeat, error, and session-end signals
examples.source_note: This is a SUPPORT ITEM, not a claim. It describes what the pipeline did — it belongs as evidence under the 'I owned the VideoViewEvents pipeline' claim, not as a standalone claim.

examples.label: rejected
examples.claim_text: Cross-midnight plays required explicit handling in the pipeline logic
examples.source_note: This is a SUB-DETAIL, not a claim. It's a specific technical constraint that belongs nested under a support item about the VideoViewEvents pipeline.

examples.label: rejected
examples.claim_text: This demonstrates strong data engineering skills across multiple cloud platforms
examples.source_note: Summary conclusion masquerading as a claim. 'Demonstrates' is a dead giveaway — it's summarizing, not asserting.

examples.label: approved
examples.claim_text: At BritBox, I worked with the GA4 BigQuery export and was the person analysts came to for queries on that data
examples.source_note: Ownership claim — not primary owner but a named role ('the person analysts came to'). Employer-specific, specific dataset.

examples.label: approved
examples.claim_text: At UNITE HERE, I built and owned custom BI reports and dashboards in SSRS, Power BI, and Sisense delivered across at least 40 locals throughout the international union
examples.source_note: Ownership + scale claim — specific tools, specific scope, employer-grounded

examples.label: rejected
examples.claim_text: I built a layered and branched architecture for handling voterfile data at Universe
examples.source_note: Borderline — this is close to a support item. 'Layered and branched architecture' is the implementation detail of the dbt environment build. Should be support under 'I built the dbt environment from scratch at Universe'.
examples.note: This one is close — if the paragraph is specifically about architecture decisions it might be a valid claim. Context-dependent.

examples.label: approved
examples.claim_text: At BritBox, I built an observation and discovery suite using DynamoDB tables feeding into DuckDB to track data quality and catch late or incomplete Amazon data
examples.source_note: Ownership + build claim — specific tool combination, specific purpose, employer-grounded. The GA4 event_params detail would be a sub-detail under a support item here, not part of the claim itself.

examples.label: approved
examples.claim_text: I am both deeply thoughtful about non-technical users and stakeholders, and serious about building solid, well-typed, tested Python
examples.source_note: APPROACH/METHOD claim — describes a specific and unusual combination (technical rigor + stakeholder orientation). Provable with specific systems built and specific stakeholder interactions from the library. Not a capability statement — it describes a WAY of working.

examples.label: approved
examples.claim_text: I spent years caring for data where precision and certainty were non-negotiable, and that intensive accountability is rare for data engineers — it shaped how I think about governance
examples.source_note: DISPOSITION/CHARACTER claim — specific assertion about professional standing grounded in real work history. Provable by showing the specific campaign data work and the accountability scope. Not just 'I care about data quality' — it asserts rarity and a specific formative experience.

examples.label: approved
examples.claim_text: I am most excited by work where careful engineering makes organizations more accountable, resilient, and effective — especially where better tooling helps good people do their work with more clarity
examples.source_note: MOTIVATION/ORIENTATION claim — specific about what KIND of work and what it produces. Not just 'passionate about data' — it names a specific outcome (organizations more accountable) and a specific mechanism (careful engineering + tooling). This is a real orientation, provable by the kinds of roles chosen.

examples.label: approved
examples.claim_text: Working backwards from what someone needs to understand into the data model that produces it is the hardest part of this work — and the part most often skipped
examples.source_note: APPROACH/METHOD claim — describes a specific professional method and a strong opinion about the work. Provable across employers (the BritBox watch-duration definition work, the UNITE HERE requirements translation) — this is not just said, it's demonstrated.

examples.label: rejected
examples.claim_text: I care about data quality
examples.source_note: Pure self-description with no specific assertion. Not provable — it's just said. The valid version names a specific formative experience and claims a specific professional standing (like gs_022). 'I care about X' is never a valid claim.

examples.label: rejected
examples.claim_text: I am passionate about data engineering
examples.source_note: Generic motivation statement with no specific orientation. Not provable. The valid version names what KIND of work matters and why (like gs_023). 'Passionate about X' without specifics is not a claim.

notes: Add new examples as patterns emerge from labeling sessions. Failure categories: too_generic, capability_statement, wrong_context_type, should_be_support_item, should_be_sub_detail, summary_not_claim, resume_speak, negative_framing, hallucinated. Claim types: (1) employer-specific ownership, (2) cross-employer thesis, (3) approach/method, (4) disposition/character, (5) motivation/orientation, (6) personal project.
